Female hogchokers attain a maximum total length of 26.8 centimeters [Li = 26.8 centimeters], a measurement that reflects the species' modest size among Northeastern American soleids. This ultimate length, observed in older individuals, is considerably larger than the size at which reproductive maturation occurs, indicating a substantial post-puberty growth phase. Field surveys in estuarine habitats along the Atlantic coast have consistently documented that females reach sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 5.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5.3 centimeters], a threshold typically achieved around two years of age. The onset of puberty at this relatively small size suggests an early commitment to reproduction, a life-history strategy common among small-bodied flatfishes that face high predation pressure. The pronounced difference between length at puberty and ultimate length, spanning over 21 centimeters, underscores a considerable period of continued physical development following the initiation of reproductive capability, allowing these fish to increase fecundity with age and size.

The wet mass of newly hatched larvae is a critical parameter for understanding early-life energetics, and for this species, it is exceptionally low. This minimal initial mass is typical of species that produce numerous small, pelagic eggs, as the hogchoker does during its spawning season. The yolk-sac larvae are entirely lecithotrophic, absorbing yolk nutrients throughout the first several days post-hatching before making the trophic switch to exogenous feeding. The small birth mass imposes a narrow energetic margin for error: larvae must successfully locate suitable prey within a short window after yolk absorption completion, or they risk reaching the point of no return. This constraint likely exerts strong selective pressure on spawning timing to coincide with peaks in planktonic food availability in estuarine environments.

In contrast to the minute mass at hatching, adult female hogchokers can reach a substantial ultimate wet weight. This ultimate wet weight is achieved through a long period of post-pubertal growth, as the weight at puberty is considerably less than the maximum. At the onset of gonadal activation, females typically have a wet weight at puberty of 2.14 grams [Wwp = 2.14 grams], marking the point at which they become capable of contributing to the next generation. The nearly 150-fold increase in body mass from puberty to ultimate size reflects a significant investment in body growth alongside reproductive effort. This pattern is common among iteroparous fishes, where larger body size confers a direct fecundity advantage, as clutch size scales positively with maternal volume and available coelomic space for developing oocytes.

The 19 °C [T = 19 °C] thermal regime employed in these experiments is representative of summer water temperatures in many mid-Atlantic estuaries, suggesting that wild populations may achieve comparable reproductive rates during peak thermal periods when prey is abundant.

Longevity records for the hogchoker indicate a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] when maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] in laboratory conditions. This extended lifespan relative to body size is noteworthy among small flatfishes, as many comparably sized estuarine species rarely exceed six to eight years. The combination of early maturation at a total length of 5.3 centimeters [Lp = 5.3 centimeters] and a long reproductive window spanning up to a decade permits females to accumulate substantial lifetime fecundity despite their relatively modest peak body mass of 315 grams [Wwi = 315 grams]. This life-history architecture positions Trinectes maculatus as a moderately long-lived, iteroparous species well suited to the variable conditions of its estuarine environment.
